en: The Dharma Gate of Mahāyāna Śamatha and Vipaśyanā, Volume One.
The Essential Mind-Instructions Transmitted by Master Sīta of Nan-yu.

Regarding the Dharma Gate of Mahāyāna Śamatha and Vipaśyanā for practitioners: if one wishes to cultivate it, one should study it within the section on the "Characteristics of the Substance of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā" below. If there is anything... [text continues]
If doubts remain unresolved, one should then read through the texts extensively; therein will surely be found the points that sever such doubts.
Furthermore, all that is elucidated here is based entirely upon the sūtras and śāstras.
Among these, there are many scriptural passages and treatise verses;
they must not be handled impurely,
for fear of incurring the sin of irreverence.
Someone asked a śramaṇa:
"Now, while those who receive their nature possess this same substance, their cultivation differs.
It is simply that because the artisan's carving varies, the vessels produced are not uniform."
I have heard that the Great Virtuous One has penetrated the ultimate principle and discerned the profound and vast doctrine; therefore,
I offer this exhortation for cultivation in the hope of hearing the True Dharma.
The śramaṇa said:
"Although I was young when I first entered the monastic life and partook of the flavor of the Way, my ignorance is deep-seated and difficult to reform;
thus, the principles of practice have not taken root within me."
"Now, I am honored by your inquiry, yet I do not know what to say.
The outsider said,
"Indeed, Venerable One, I pray that you will not disdain the labor and explain for me the practice of the Mahāyāna."
"I respectfully receive and uphold these words, not daring to forget them.
The śramaṇa said, "Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to give rise to this unsurpassed mind."
You delight in hearing the practices of the Mahāyāna;
you have now already transcended the realm of the two vehicles,
let alone desiring to hear and practice them.
Nevertheless, although one has generated this sublime resolve, its virtue must be accomplished through practice.
While the methods of practice are ten thousandfold and the ways of entering the Path are not singular,
I shall now briefly explain for you, my son, the two gates of Mahāyāna *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based upon the sūtras and śāstras.
"By relying on this Dharma, you shall quickly fulfill your aspirations.
The outsider said, "Excellent!
I pray that you will speak so as to satisfy my mind."
Furthermore, by causing other people to benefit one another in succession, one transmits the lamp of the Dharma without interruption; this is how one repays the Buddha's kindness.
The śramaṇa said:
Listen attentively and maintain careful composure; I shall explain it for you.
As for what is called "cessation" (śamatha):
it means knowing that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are by nature non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing.
It exists through false causes and conditions, yet it exists as non-existence.
However, that which exists as a phenomenon is precisely non-existent;
it is solely the substance of the one mind, devoid of discrimination.
One who practices this contemplation is able to prevent deluded thoughts from flowing; therefore,
it is called "calming" (śamatha).
As for what is called "contemplation":
although one knows that [all things] are fundamentally unborn and do not perish now,
yet because the mind-nature arises through conditions, illusory worldly functions are not non-existent.
It is like an illusion or a dream: though non-existent, it appears to exist;
therefore, it is called "contemplation.
The opponent says:
"My understanding is dull and my consciousness faint; having heard this, I have not yet been able to realize it immediately.
I pray that you will employ skillful means to explain it further.
The śramaṇa said:
Nevertheless, I shall further provide you with a detailed analysis so that those who have not yet heard it may seek it out and attain realization.
Within this extensive analysis of the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, five systematic establishments will be made.
First, the basis of śamatha and vipaśyanā is clarified;
second, the objects of śamatha and vipaśyanā are clarified; third, the essential nature and characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā are clarified.
The fourth clarifies the cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) regarding abandonment and attainment; the fifth clarifies the functional application of cessation and contemplation.
Within the first [section], that of the basis (*āśraya*), there is further a threefold analysis.
First, it clarifies what is relied upon;
second, it clarifies why one relies [upon it];
third, it clarifies by means of what one relies [upon it].
First, to clarify that upon which one relies:
it means relying upon the single mind to cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Within this, there are furthermore three types of distinctions.
First, the title of the work;
second, the explanation of its meaning;
third, the discernment of its essential nature.
Regarding the first, the name "that which emerges from the multitude":
this mind is precisely the intrinsically pure mind (prakṛti-viśuddha-citta),
and it is also named True Suchness (tathatā).
It is also called Buddha-nature,
further termed the Dharma-body,
and likewise referred to as the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is also called the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and further named the Dharma-nature (dharmatā);
such names as these are immeasurable and boundless.
Therefore, the various names have been stated.
Next, the meaning of these names will be analyzed and explained. Question:
What is called the intrinsically pure mind?
The answer is:
although this mind has, from beginningless time, been shrouded by the defiled dharmas of ignorance, [it remains intrinsically pure].
Yet its nature is pure and unchanging;
therefore, it is called "pure. Why is this?
The defiled dharmas of ignorance are fundamentally dissociated from the mind.
How are they dissociated?
This means that because the essence of ignorance is a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāva-dharma*), it is not existent;
and because it is not existent, it cannot be associated with the mind.
Therefore, it is said to be "detached. Since there is no defiled phenomenon of ignorance with which it could be associated, [it is detached].
Therefore, it is called "pure by nature.
Because it is the true, central, primordial awakening (mūla-awakening), it is called "mind" (citta).
Thus, it is termed the "intrinsically pure mind" (prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta).
Question: What is meant by "True Suchness" (tathatā)? Answer:
All phenomena depend upon this mind and take the mind as their essence.
In relation to all phenomena, they are entirely illusory; though they appear to exist, they do not truly exist.
In contrast to these deceptive phenomena, [the mind is real].
Therefore, it is designated as "real.
Furthermore, although all phenomena do not truly exist,
they nonetheless manifest the characteristics of arising and ceasing through false causes and conditions.
However, when those empty phenomena arise, this mind does not arise;
when all phenomena cease, this mind does not cease.
Because it does not arise, it does not increase; because it does not cease, it does not decrease.
Because it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing,
it is called "True. This applies to all Buddhas of the three periods of time as well as to sentient beings.
All share this same single pure mind as their essence;
while all phenomena of ordinary beings and sages possess their own distinct differences and characteristics,
this true mind is without differentiation and without marks.
Therefore, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Furthermore, as for True Suchness:
because all phenomena are truly thus and are solely this one mind.
Therefore, this single mind is named *tathatā* (suchness).
If there were dharmas external to the mind,
they would not be real, nor would it be so.
This would then be a false distinction between characteristics.
Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression."
It is free from the characteristics of names and free from the characteristics of mental objects;
it is ultimately equal, without change or variation,
and indestructible.
Because it is solely this one mind, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
For this reason, the intrinsically pure mind is further named *tathatā*. Question:
Why, furthermore, is this mind called Buddha-nature?
The answer is:
"Buddha" means awakening, and "nature" means mind.
Because the substance of this pure mind is not non-awakening,
it is called the awakening mind. Question:
How is it known that this true mind is not non-awakening?
The answer is:
non-awakening is precisely the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
If this pure mind were ignorance, then when sentient beings attain Buddhahood and ignorance is extinguished, there would be no true mind. Why is this?
Because the mind is ignorance,
once that ignorance has naturally ceased, the pure mind becomes sovereign;
therefore, one knows that the pure mind is not non-awakening.
Furthermore, it is because one realizes non-awakening that one subsequently attains a pure mind;
thus, one comes to know that the mind is not without awakening.
A question is asked:
Why not define awakening as such by virtue of its own nature being awakening?
Why instead say it is called awakening because it is not non-awakening?
The answer is:
The essence of the mind is equal, being neither awakening nor non-awakening;
however, in order to clarify the Buddha of Suchness (Tathatā), it is provisionally described as awakening for the sake of correspondence.
Therefore, the sutra says:
"There is no nirvana for all;
there is no Buddha who has entered nirvana, nor is there a nirvana belonging to a Buddha."

To be far removed from both existence and non-existence regarding the perceiver and the perceived—this is to be entirely free from these two; this is explained specifically in terms of the equality of the essence of mind.
If, however, one explains "awakening" (bodhi) by way of the functional significance of the mind-essence as the *dharmadhātu*:
This essence of mind possesses three kinds of great wisdom, namely:
unlearned wisdom, spontaneous wisdom, and... [wisdom].
Unobstructed wisdom.
This awakened mind-essence is inherently endowed with the nature of these three wisdoms;
therefore, this mind is taken as the nature of awakening.
Therefore, one must understand the meaning of identity and difference. What is identity?
It means that the essence of the mind is equal, which is itself wisdom-awakening.
The awakening of wisdom is precisely the equality of the essence of mind;
therefore, it is said they are the same. Furthermore, how could they be different?
That is to say, the meaning of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) is its function;
in ordinary beings it is called Buddha-nature,
and it is also termed the nature of the three kinds of wisdom.
That which emerges from hindrances is called the Buddha of Wisdom.
The meaning of the equality of the essence of mind is the substance;
therefore, there is no duality between ordinary beings and sages, and it is designated solely as the Buddha of Suchness.
Therefore, one should understand that they are distinct in this way.
Question: What is meant by "the Buddha of wisdom"?
Because he is able to awaken the pure mind,
he is called a Buddha;
because he has self-awakened the pure mind, he is so named.
Therefore, he is named Buddha.
The answer is:
it possesses two meanings.
First is awakening to the pure mind;
second is the pure mind’s self-awakening.
Although these two meanings are spoken of, their essence is not distinct.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that when all Buddhas were originally in the state of ordinary beings,
their minds— relying on perfuming and undergoing transformation— moved spontaneously through non-awakening, manifesting illusory appearances.
That which is of a false appearance refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) of ordinary beings;
it is also termed "resembling consciousness," "resembling form," and "resembling sense objects."
That which resembles consciousness refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
It is because these resembling consciousnesses arise moment by moment that [the storehouse consciousness is so designated].
That is to say, one does not understand that phenomena appearing as form and so forth are merely the mind’s construction of empty marks devoid of reality; because of this lack of understanding,
one falsely clings to these empty marks as if they were real entities.
At the time of false attachment, it immediately perfumes the pure mind in return.
However, the meaning of the semblance-consciousness’s lack of realization is precisely ignorance at the stage of the fruit.
It is also called ignorance regarding deluded objects.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because of delusion (*moha*) with respect to conditions, consciousness falsely clings to [the appearance of] objects."
That is to say, the objects grasped by deluded conceptualization become delusory realms themselves.
This is because, at the stage of fruition, ignorance perfumes the mind,
causing the mind to lack awakening.
This is precisely the time of midnight; ignorance is also called the "ground-abiding ignorance" (*mūlasthāny-avidyā*).
Because deluded conceptualization perfumes the mind, it causes the mind to fluctuate;
this is the "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*).
Because false objects permeate the mind, they cause the mind to become seeds resembling objects;
because what resembles consciousness permeates the mind, they cause the mind to become seeds resembling consciousness.
These two types of seeds—those resembling objects and those resembling consciousness—...
Collectively, these are termed "illusory-seed-phenomena.
However, although it is said that at the time of fruition, ignorance and the other factors each separately perfume to give rise to a single dharma,
they must be in simultaneous conjunction in order to function as perfumers.
Why is this? Because they exist in mutual dependence through their inseparable characteristics;
if there were no semblance of consciousness, then at the time of the fruit, ignorance would not exist.
If there were no ignorance, there would be no deluded conceptualization;
if there were no deluded conceptualization, deluded objects would not be established.
Therefore, it is only through the simultaneous conjunction of these four factors that the fruit of illusory appearances can manifest.
Why is this? Because they are not separate.
Furthermore, the seeds of empty appearances abide in ignorance at the time of those seeds.
Furthermore, because the seeds of empty appearances cannot manifest a fruit alone:
if there were no seeds, then ignorance would be without the karma-consciousness;
and if there were no karma-consciousness, then the seeds of empty appearances could not manifest and produce a fruit.
Thus, the self-substance itself cannot be established.
Therefore, it is only through combination that the illusory appearance of a fruit manifests.
Consequently, within this illusory fruit, there still exist the false ignorance and deluded attachments that resemble consciousness and resemble objects.
For this reason, it is briefly described as "non-awakening";
thus, movement manifests as illusory forms.
In this manner, the mutual generation of seeds and fruits in a beginningless cycle of transmigration is termed "sentient beings."
Later, he encountered a virtuous friend who explained to him that all phenomena are produced by the single mind and appear as if they exist,
though they are not real. Having heard this teaching,
he practiced in accordance with it and gradually came to know that all phenomena are produced from the mind alone, being merely empty and devoid of reality.
When this understanding is established, it is the time of the fruit, at which point ignorance ceases.
Because ignorance ceases, one no longer clings to illusory appearances as real;
this is the cessation of both deluded conceptualization and its deluded objects.
At that time, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is renamed "wisdom free from objects" (*anartha-jñāna*),
because it knows that objects have no reality. Nevertheless,
because it knows that the objective realm is empty, it is said that at the time of the fruit, ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished.
It is like perceiving the existence of empty appearances;
yet that which exists is non-existent, for its fundamental nature is neither born nor does it now perish.
It is solely this one mind, yet because one does not understand this principle, [delusion arises].
Therefore, it is also called the ignorance of the "time of the son" (subconscious ignorance),
and it is also called the ignorance that is deluded regarding principle;
however, it is subtler than the aforementioned ignorance that is deluded regarding phenomena.
Because that which is coarse has ceased, it is said that at the time of the fruit, ignorance ceases.
Furthermore, because one does not grasp at empty appearances as real,
it is said that delusive conceptualization ceases.
To still perceive the appearance of emptiness while claiming there is a distinct mind—
this attachment is likewise a false conception and is also termed an "appearance of emptiness."
However, it is subtler than the former because that [former] has been extinguished through its coarseness; thus it is said that "delusive discrimination is extinguished.
Furthermore, this empty object is grasped by the subtle ignorance and delusive discrimination that still exist.
That which appears to have characteristics different from the mind, yet whose characteristics are not identical to it, is a delusive object.
However, because it is subtler than the former, it is called a "void" object.
Furthermore, because the attachment to its coarse characteristics as real has ceased, it is said that the delusive object has ceased.
Judging by this, it is not merely that ignorance regarding phenomena ceases at the time of fruition;
even the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is partially eliminated.
If it were not eliminated bit by bit and gradually, [it could not be so].
At the time of fruition, ignorance cannot be extinguished part by part in a gradual manner;
rather, its manifestations become so subtle that they are difficult to manifest.
For this reason, it is not said that it is extinguished stage by stage within the ground.
For now, let us consider the gradual extinction of the ground-dwelling ignorance (*bhūmi-stha-avidyā*) following the cessation of deluded phenomenal ignorance (*vastu-avidyā*).
By means of this, one should understand that from the very moment a single thought-moment of cultivation is initiated, it is also capable of being gradually extinguished.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that by virtue of two causal conditions,
the ignorance residing in the ground (*ālayavijñāna*), the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), and so forth, gradually become attenuated and subtle.
What are these two meanings?
First, because the knowledge that perceives objects as empty permeates the mind,
it causes the habitual tendencies of the long-standing ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) to be gradually eliminated.
Why is this? Because wisdom is clarity;
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is able to remedy ignorance.
Second, because the subtle ignorance, false attachments, and false objects permeate the mind,
even though the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) and so forth arise again,
they are light and weak, unlike those [afflictions] previously produced through permeation by deluded objects and the like.
Why is this? Because the perfuming is subtle,
the resulting non-awakening is likewise attenuated.
For this reason, the ignorance residing in the ground (*mūla-avidyā*), the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), and so forth, are gradually diminished and extinguished.
Since this principle applies once the ignorance regarding phenomena (*vastu-avidyā*) has been extinguished.
It should be understood that at the very moment one first initiates the practice, the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) is partially extinguished.
Because it is extinguished part by part,
the wisdom that arises increases in clarity part by part.
Therefore, at the time of attaining the fruit, the ignorance regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha-avidyā*) is extinguished.
Following the extinction of this ignorance regarding phenomena, the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and the fundamental ignorance (*ālaya-avidyā*) gradually thin out.
Consequently, the illusory manifestations of karmic retribution that arise also become increasingly subtle and refined, no longer being as they were previously.
For this reason, the transformation of what resembles consciousness becomes increasingly clear and sharp,
and that which resembles dharmas such as form no longer causes confusion to arise in the mental consciousness.
Because the internal consciousness arises together with external objects such as forms, both being subtle and sharp,
the wisdom that is free from objects becomes doubly luminous; thus,
ignorance and false conceptualization become extremely thin and revert to perfuming the mind once again.
Furthermore, as the habitual tendencies of the karma-consciousness of ignorance residing in the ground gradually tend toward exhaustion,
the wisdom that manifests in the absence of objects becomes doubly luminous;
this is because such [wisdom] is understood through the successive, moment-to-moment permeation of cultivation.
Arising from the near-exhaustion of the ground of abiding ignorance,
the dustless wisdom is able to know that the nature of the body of those empty-form karmic results is non-existent and fundamentally unborn;
it is now without cessation.
It is solely the essence of the one mind, devoid of discrimination,
because there are no phenomena external to the mind alone.
This wisdom is precisely the unimpeded vajra-wisdom.
Once this wisdom is perfected, it in turn perfumes the mind.
Because the mind is perfumed by clear wisdom,
the habitual tendencies of ignorance within a single thought-moment are immediately extinguished, and ignorance is exhausted.
Therefore, the seeds and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the defiled dharmas within the *karma-vijñāna* are likewise destroyed.
For this reason, the Sūtra says:
"When that earth is destroyed, those [seeds] are also destroyed along with it."
This is precisely its meaning:
because the seeds and habitual tendencies are destroyed,
the illusory appearances are forever extinguished.
Because empty forms have vanished, the essence of mind is quiescent yet luminous;
this is called the realization of the essence of True Suchness (tathatā). Why is this so?
Because it takes non-differentiation as its means of realization,
it is a state of tranquil illumination wherein there is no distinction between the realizing subject and the realized object;
this is termed non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Why is this? Because apart from this wisdom, there is no separate suchness (tathatā) that can be discerned;
this very mind is manifested as wisdom.
Wisdom is the function of the mind;
the mind is the substance of wisdom.
Substance and function are a single dharma, their self-nature being non-dual.
Therefore, it is called the realization of the essence of self-nature.
It is like still water that reflects inwardly; although the meanings of "reflecting" and "moistening" differ, it remains perpetually serene and one. Why is this so?
Because illumination moistens and moisture illuminates,
the mind is likewise:
though its meanings of stillness and illumination are distinct, their essence is harmoniously fused and non-dual.
Why is this? Because it illuminates stillness through stillness and illuminates through illumination.
Illuminating stillness accords with the essence; illuminating through illumination accords with function.
The illumination of its own essence is called awakening (*bodhi*).
When the essence of the pure mind illuminates itself, it is called the pure mind.
Because it is self-awakened, these two meanings are said to be one essence.
This means that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) itself constitutes awakening.
The pure mind has possessed this nature from the very beginning;
the essence of wisdom neither increases nor decreases.
Therefore, the pure mind is taken as the Buddha-nature.
This explains that the pure mind constitutes the Buddha-nature from the perspective of the Wisdom-Buddha.
Furthermore, this pure mind inherently possesses the nature of merit and the nature of skillful application.
Furthermore, because it is perfumed by pure karma, it gives rise to the two Buddhas of retribution and response;
therefore, this mind is taken as the Buddha-nature.
Moreover, because it is not aware of its own cessation, the mind is taken as awakening.
Because the meaning of movement has ceased, it is said that the mind is unmoving;
because delusive appearances have vanished, it is said that the mind is signless.
Nevertheless, the essence of this mind is neither awakening nor non-awakening.
It is neither moving nor non-moving;
it is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics.
Nevertheless, because non-awakening has been extinguished, the mind is said to be awakening.
Nor is there any contradiction here.
This discussion concerns awakening (*bodhi*) in terms of the essential nature of the mind that emerges from obstacles through the application of remedies;
it does not rely upon the functional activity of wisdom (*jñāna*) as being awakening.
Furthermore, the pure mind is fundamentally without non-awakening;
it is taught that the mind is fundamental awakening, fundamentally without movement or change, and is taught that the mind is fundamentally quiescent.
It is fundamentally without illusory marks, and the mind is said to be fundamentally equal.
However, the essence of that mind is neither awakening nor non-awakening;
neither movement nor non-movement;
neither with characteristics nor without characteristics.
Although it is called "original awakening" (mūla-bodhi) because there is no non-awakening within original nature,
there is likewise nothing lost thereby.
This is explained from the perspective of the non-duality of ordinary beings and sages,
clarifying that the essence of mind is the Tathāgata;
it does not concern itself with the function of the innate, awakened nature inherent within the essence of mind.
Question: If awakening consists in the absence of non-awakening within the fundamental nature, then ordinary beings are already Buddhas;
what need is there for the cultivation of the path?
The answer is:
If one approaches it from the perspective of the equality of the essence of mind,
there is neither cultivation nor non-cultivation, neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment.
Furthermore, there is neither awakening nor non-awakening;
it is only for the sake of clarifying the Buddha of Suchness that awakening is posited as a conceptual counterpart.
Moreover, if one relies upon the equality of the essence of mind, [there is no distinction].
Furthermore, there are no sentient beings distinct from this essence of mind within which all Buddhas reside.
Thus, a verse in a sutra says:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction."
Furthermore, the mind-nature, dependent origination, and the dharma-realm are the natural,
indestructible nature of the Dharma-gate; therefore,
they are eternally equal and eternally distinct.
Because they are eternally equal, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three—are without distinction.
Because they are eternally differentiated, those who circulate through the five realms of existence are called sentient beings;
those who reverse the flow and exhaust the source are called Buddhas.
Because this meaning of equality exists,
there is neither Buddha nor sentient being;
yet because this meaning of the differentiation of dependent origination exists, [there is].
Sentient beings must cultivate the Way.
Question: How can it be known that the substance of the mind is fundamentally non-awakened?
The answer is:
If non-awakening were inherently present within the substance of the mind,
then when a sage realizes the pure mind, they should no longer experience non-awakening.
Ordinary beings have not yet realized that which ought to be realized.
Once realization has been attained, there is no one who is not awakened.
One who has not yet realized it cannot be called awakened.
Therefore, it is certain that the substance of the mind is fundamentally devoid of non-awakening. Question:
Do the sages extinguish non-awakening?
Therefore, one attains the pure mind of self-realization.
If there were no lack of awakening,
how could one speak of cessation?
Furthermore, if there were no non-awakening, there would be no sentient beings.
The answer is:
this has already been fully explained above.
The essence of the mind is equal, being neither ordinary nor sagely; therefore,
it is said that there is fundamentally no non-enlightenment,
yet the nature of the mind as dependent origination is not non-existent.
Therefore, there is cessation, there is realization, there are ordinary beings, and there are noble ones.
Furthermore, the existence of dependent origination is such that existence is itself non-existence.
Therefore, it is said that originally there was no non-awakening,
and now likewise there is no non-awakening; yet this does not mean that [awakening] is not present.
Therefore, it is said that there is cessation, there is realization, there are ordinary beings, and there are sages.
However, when realization functions in accordance with the essence itself, there is no lack of awakening.
Thus, one can verify that the substance of the mind is fundamentally devoid of non-awakening.
However, whenever one uses the notion of "identity" in a contrary way by asserting "difference," one cannot thereby realize the essence of equality.
[The opponent] asks:
If it is argued that the mind, when manifested as wisdom, is [tainted] by the dust of ignorance,
and therefore this natural wisdom must have some other distinct causes and conditions,
the answer is:
When this mind is in a state of defilement,
it inherently possesses the two natures of merit and wisdom without lacking even one; thus,
the dharmas and the Buddha are no different.
However, because it is shrouded by the defiled phenomena of ignorance,
its functional manifestation cannot be revealed;
subsequently, it is perfumed by the two kinds of pure karma— merit and wisdom.
Therefore, all defiled phenomena are completely exhausted.
However, when this pure activity eliminates defilement,
it is immediately able to manifest those two natures.

This brings about functional efficacy, namely the marks and embellishments (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), the environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), and all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
The essence of wisdom is itself the capacity of the true mind’s intrinsic illumination; the functional application of wisdom is formed through perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Question: If it is held that when the mind manifests as wisdom, the mind itself constitutes the Buddha-nature,
then when the mind arises as non-awakening, the mind should likewise constitute the nature of ignorance.
The answer is:
If one discusses this from the perspective of the meaning of *dharmatā*,
it can also be considered the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Wisdom and ignorance are non-dual in their nature;
this non-dual nature is itself the true nature."
Question: Why is this mind called the "Dharmakāya"? Answer:
"Dharma" has the meaning of functional capacity;
"body" (kāya) has the meaning of a basis.
This is because this essence of mind possesses the function of conforming to defilement.
It is perfumed by all defiled dharmas;
because this mind follows along with defilement,
it is able to retain the latent impressions of that perfuming.
Furthermore, it can manifest defiled phenomena based on perfuming; thus,
this very nature of mind possesses two functional capacities— namely, the capacity to sustain and the capacity to manifest—
as well as the two types of defiled phenomena that are sustained and manifested.
All [phenomena] are established based upon this single mind.
Because it is neither identical to nor different from the mind, this mind is termed the *dharmakāya*.
The functional capacity that sustains [all things] and the vital energy sustained therein are in harmonious union.
Therefore, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* of the causal moment (*bīja-kāla*).
Because the capacity to manifest phenomena through perfuming (*vāsanā*) and the manifested images (*nimitta*) are conjoined,
it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* of retribution (*vipāka*).
These two consciousnesses are identical in essence but differ in function.
Furthermore, within this ālayavijñāna there are two divisions:
the first is the defiled division.
This refers to the characteristics of karma and its retribution.
Second is the pure portion,
which consists of the nature of the mind and the purifying dharmas that can perfuse it.
It is called the "pure portion" because its defiled nature is itself the pure nature, with no separate dharma existing between them. Therefore,
this mind-nature serves as the basis for those defiled phenomena that are the fruits of karma.
Therefore, it is said that birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*;
this is precisely the *dharmakāyagarbha*.
Furthermore, although the essence of this mind is shrouded by immeasurable defiled phenomena, [it remains inherently pure].
Furthermore, it is fully endowed with merit-dharmas of the untainted nature (anāsrava) exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
it is perfumed by immeasurable pure karma.
Therefore, this pure nature is able to sustain the scent of these perfumations.
Furthermore, it is able to manifest the function of various pure merits based upon these perfumings;
that is to say, these sands-of-the-Ganges-like inherently pure merits,
along with the two types of functional capacities— the capacity to sustain and the capacity to manifest.
Furthermore, both the two kinds of pure functions— the supported and the manifested—
rely entirely upon this single mind for their establishment;
they are neither identical to nor different from the mind.
Therefore, this mind is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Question:
Why, furthermore, is this mind called the Tathāgatagarbha?
The answer is that there are three meanings.
First, that which is capable of concealing is called "store" (ālaya).
Second, that which is concealed is called "store."
Third is that which can produce the treasury of names.
Regarding that which can store,
there are further two kinds.
First is the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s fruition-virtue;
second is the pure mind of the sentient beings’ nature-virtue.
Both are capable of encompassing both the natures of defilement and purity, as well as the phenomena of defilement and purity, without any mutual obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that that which is capable of concealing is called the "store" (ālaya).
The equality of the essence of this store is termed "suchness" (tathatā).
This equality of dependent origination is designated as "coming" (āgata).
This is what is called the "Tathāgatagarbha" in the sense of that which is capable of concealing;
secondly, regarding the "garbha" in the sense of that which is concealed, it refers to this very true mind being covered and concealed by the shell of ignorance.
Therefore, it is called that which is "stored.
The essence of this store is without differentiation and without marks; it is termed "Suchness" (tathatā).
Its essence fully possesses the two functions of defilement and purity; it is designated as "coming" (āgama).
Therefore, it is said that what is stored is called a "store" (*garbha*).
Regarding the third point, that which is capable of producing is called a "store":
just as a woman's womb (*garbha*) is capable of producing a child.
This mind is likewise;
its essence possesses the functional capacity for both defiled and pure natures.
Therefore, it relies upon the two types of perfuming power—defiled and pure.
It is capable of producing both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha..."
This is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The nature of the mind is one."
How is it that various karmic fruits and retributions can be produced?
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The ocean of the Buddhas' perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind and its perceptions."
Therefore, the equality of defilement and purity is termed "Suchness" (tathatā).
That which can give rise to defilement and purity is designated as "coming" (āgata).
Thus, it is said that that which can give rise [to these] is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
Question: Why is the purified mind further called the dharma-realm? Answer:
"Dharma" means that it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*);
"realm" (*dhātu*) means that it is the differentiation of natures.
Thus, this essence of mind is by its very nature endowed with all dharmas.
Therefore, it is called the *dharmadhātu*. Question:
Why is this pure mind designated as the *dharmatā*?
The answer is:
"Dharma" refers to all phenomena;
"nature" (svabhāva) has the meaning of distinct essence.
Because this pure mind possesses a nature characterized by differentiation,
it is able to serve as the essence (svabhāva) of all phenomena.
Furthermore, "nature" (prakṛti) carries the meaning of being a real entity that is unchanging.
Since all phenomena take this mind as their essence,
while the characteristics of these phenomena inherently possess arising and ceasing,
they are therefore termed "illusory."
This mind is truly unchanging and indestructible;
therefore, it is called the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature).
Other infinite designations, such as the "actual limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) and "true mark" (*lakṣaṇa*), cannot be fully explained here.
The explanation of the definitions and meanings is now complete.
Next, the essential nature and characteristics will be set forth.
As for what is called "essential nature and characteristics":
Within this, there are furthermore three kinds of distinctions:
first, to clarify the pure mind by citing its characteristic of detachment;
second, to discuss the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) by citing its neither-identity-nor-difference.
The three citations of the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha serve to distinguish True Suchness (tathatā).
Although there are three distinct types,
they collectively elucidate only the essential nature and characteristics of this pure mind.
First, regarding the clarification of being free from marks:
this mind is precisely the ultimate truth, the *tathatā*-mind.
Its self-nature is perfectly interfused, its essence fully endowed with great function.
However, it is that which is known through the noble wisdom of self-realization,
and cannot be fathomed by the measures of ordinary intellect;
therefore, it is said:
The path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished;
it cannot be named by names,
nor can it be characterized by marks.
Why is this? Because the essence of the mind is free from names and characteristics.
Since its essence is already free from names, one cannot employ names to discuss that essence.
Since the mind has already transcended all characteristics, it is impossible to discern that mind by means of its characteristics.
Therefore, if one now wishes to discuss its essential nature and form, it is indeed difficult;
one can only speak of the characteristics from which it is free.
By reversing the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of cessation, one attains personal realization therein.
That which is called this mind has, from the very beginning,
been free from all characteristics, being equanimous and quiescently extinguished.
Neither having marks nor lacking marks;
neither not having marks nor not lacking marks;
neither both having and lacking marks.
It is also without marks;
it is neither past, future, nor present;
it is neither superior, middling, nor inferior.
Neither that nor this;
neither stillness nor agitation, neither defilement nor purity;
neither eternalism nor nihilism.
Neither light nor darkness;
neither one nor different, and so forth—
this is a general exposition of all dharmas categorized within the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).
This extends even to those phenomena that are neither expressible nor conceivable,
nor are they inexpressible or inconceivable. Why is this?
Because that which is inexpressible and inconceivable arises as a phenomenon that is not its own intrinsic nature in contrast to that which is expressible and conceivable,
it is therefore not the pure mind; thus, one only knows all that is expressible and conceivable.
Ineffable and inconceivable phenomena and so forth are all not the pure mind itself;
they are merely illusory appearances manifested by the pure mind.
However, these empty marks each lack their own substantial reality; that which exists is precisely non-existent.
Even the mark of non-existence cannot be grasped. Why is this so?
Because that which has no original existence does not exist. If there is no original existence,
how could there be the characteristic of non-existence?
Therefore, one should know that the essence of the pure mind cannot be known through discursive thought and cannot be reached by verbal expression.
Why is this? Because there is not a single dharma apart from the pure mind.
If there are no dharmas apart from the mind, [then...]
Furthermore, who else could perceive or describe this mind?
Therefore, one should know that all those who can perceive and describe [it]—
However, they are false and unreal;
therefore, upon examination, they are found to be non-existent.
Since the subjective perceiver is not real, how could the objective object perceived be real?
Because both the subjective perceiver and the objective perceived are entirely unreal, the pure mind—being a real dharma—is not something to be known through cognitive apprehension.
For example, the eye cannot see itself; it requires another eye external to this one.
This eye that is able to see consists of both one's own eye and another's eye;
the mind is not like this.
It is simply suchness (tathatā).
Apart from suchness, there are no dharmas.
Furthermore, the pure mind does not engage in self-discrimination.
How could there be anyone capable of discerning and grasping this mind?
For those ordinary people who deludedly attempt to discern the pure mind are like foolish men who, with eyes wide open, search for their own eyes.
Furthermore, they claim that various appearances are their own eyes,
yet they do not know the locus of their own eyes.
Therefore, one should understand this.
There is that which can take an object as its support;
however, this is merely one's own family of pure minds,
permeated by beginningless false conceptualization.
Therefore, being unable to know their own nature,
they give rise to false discrimination and establish the appearance of a pure mind external to their own minds.
Yet, one again grasps at these through deluded conceptualization, taking them to be a pure mind.
To examine the reality of the matter,
the characteristics thus grasped are precisely the characteristics of consciousness.
In truth, it is not the pure mind itself.
[The questioner] asks:
What is the essence of the pure mind?
Since it cannot be differentiated in the same way as all sentient beings,
how can one accord with it and thereby gain entry?
The answer is:
If one knows that the essence of all deluded thoughts and discriminations is the pure mind,
yet because these discriminations do not cease, they are said to be contrary to principle.
Having gained this knowledge, one should contemplate all phenomena:
that all conditioned thoughts exist yet are non-existent;
therefore, it is called "conformity."
If, after long-term cultivation, one is free from conceptual discrimination,
it is called "attaining entry";
this is precisely the direct realization of *tathatā* (suchness) by transcending all signs.
This concludes the first section, which clarifies the nature and characteristics by means of the absence of marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Next, the nature and characteristics are clarified through the principle of being neither identical nor different.
Although it has been explained above that the pure mind is free from all conceptualizing minds and the marks of objective realms, [the following further elucidates this].
Nevertheless, these various marks are not different from the pure mind.
Why is this? Although the essence of this mind is indeed impartial, [the marks arise].
Yet, it inherently possesses both the functions of defilement and purity.

Furthermore, due to the power of the habitual perfuming of beginningless ignorance and deluded thoughts, the defiled function of the mind’s essence manifests based upon this perfuming; these various illusory appearances lack substantiality and are in truth nothing but the pure mind.
Therefore, it is said that they are not different, yet they are also not one. Why is this?
Although the essence of the pure mind possesses both the functions of defilement and purity,
it lacks any characteristic of dualistic differentiation in its nature.
They are of a single flavor and equal, appearing merely as illusory marks manifested through the power of habitual perfuming;
yet they differ in their various distinctions.
Nevertheless, these illusory marks—
There is arising and there is ceasing;
however, because the essence of the pure mind is eternally without arising or ceasing, constant, and unchanging, it is said not to be "one.
This concludes the second point—neither identical nor different—used to clarify the characteristics of the essence.
Next, to clarify the third section concerning the two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha* in order to distinguish their essential characteristics:
first, we clarify the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
For what reason is it called "empty"?
Although this mind-nature establishes phenomena such as birth-and-death and nirvana, or the favorable and the adverse, through dependent origination,
the essence of the mind remains equal, wondrously transcending all marks of defilement and purity.
It does not arise from the equality of the intrinsic nature of the essence of the non-direct mind;
furthermore, phenomena such as defilement and purity are likewise non-existent by their very nature,
just like [seeking] a rabbit in a cloth.
The body of the rabbit is non-existent;
it is only through the power of illusion that it appears as a rabbit.
As for the rabbit thus manifested—
That which exists is itself non-existent.
The mind is also like this;
it is merely perfumed by the illusory power of the two types of karma—defiled and pure.
The two phenomena of defilement and purity appear as such;
yet, when viewed from the perspective of the mind,
those phenomena do not exist.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Cyclic flow is birth and death;
non-flowing is nirvāṇa."
Both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are unattainable.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
The five aggregates are like an illusion;
even up to Great Parinirvāṇa, they are like an illusion.
If there were any dharma that transcended Nirvāṇa, it too would be like an illusion.
I also say that they are like an illusion.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"There is no nirvana for anything whatsoever."
There is no Buddha apart from nirvāṇa;
there is no nirvāṇa apart from the Buddha.
It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened.
Whether there is existence or non-existence,
both are entirely transcended;
these scriptural passages all rely upon the equality of the essence of mind.
Because the two functions of defilement and purity are extinguished, the nature of the mind is quiescent;
therefore, the essence of the mind is empty and pure. For these reasons, this essence of the mind is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha."
This does not mean that the essence of the mind is empty and non-existent.
A question is asked:
"The pure mind realized as the essence of all Buddhas may be considered equal in its mental essence."
Therefore, the Buddha also employs the teaching that [phenomena] are non-existent while remaining eternally quiescent.
Since sentient beings have not yet realized the principle, they currently manifest the distinctions of the six realms; how could these be non-existent?
He replied:
Even true wisdom and true illumination—
when they employ the "immediate" as eternally quiescent— are described as emptiness;
how much more so, then, deluded darkness and false views?
How could it not exist? To exist is precisely to be non-existent.
[The opponent] asks:
Since it has been stated that they do not exist,
how can this delusion and error arise?
The answer is:
Since one perceives existence where there is no existence,
why does one not likewise perceive non-existence where there is no delusion,
yet instead gives rise to delusion arbitrarily?
The analogy of flowers in the sky is appropriately presented here.
It is asked:
"It may be said that all other defiled phenomena are non-existent."
If ignorance is the cause of defilement, how can it be non-existent? The answer is:
both types of ignorance—the causal and the resultant—fundamentally lack intrinsic nature.
It has only the pure mind as its essence;
it possesses the function of delusion solely due to the conditions of habitual perfuming.
When the mind is fully encompassed by [this purity], that function is then non-existent.
It is solely this one mind.
Just as millet and barley have no intrinsic nature of their own and have only atoms as their substance,
[the world] exists merely through the causal conditions of seeds.
Therefore, there is the use of millet and wheat;
yet when one goes to collect them by means of atoms, they are not found to exist.
It is only that these are subtle atoms. Ignorance is also like this: its existence is non-existence.
Question: Since it is said that delusive functioning exists due to the causes and conditions of perfuming (vāsanā),
the dharma that acts as the perfumer should itself constitute the essence of ignorance (avidyā).
Why is it that the pure mind takes [emptiness] as its essence?
The answer is:
although the perfuming agent can perfume others to cause [them] to arise, it itself perishes moment by moment.
How could that which arises be identical to the very substance from which it originated?
It is like a grain of barley, which can only produce fruit while its own substance decays and reverts to minute particles.
How could it be that the wheat of springtime is itself the fruit that comes from autumn?
If that were the case, the wheat of the beginning of the kalpa would still exist today in the past.
Ignorance is likewise thus:
it can only permeate and give rise to subsequent moments of ignorance;
its own substance cannot cease on its own.
This is precisely the ignorance of subsequent thought.
If this were the case, ignorance would be permanent;
for dharmas are not thought.
Since the cessation of mindfulness is not permanent,
it arises through the mutual causality of preceding and succeeding moments, like the flame of a lamp;
its essence is solely the pure mind.
Therefore, when this mind encompasses that which exists, it is immediately not-existent;
since that existence is non-existence,
this pure mind is called the "emptiness Tathāgatagarbha."
Question: At the stage of fruition, are ignorance and deluded thought one or different?
At the stage of the seed, are ignorance and karmic consciousness one or different?
The answer is:
neither identical nor different. Why is this so?
Because the pure mind does not perceive,
whatever moves is non-perceiving, which is itself non-movement.
Furthermore, if there were no ignorance, there would be no karma-consciousness.
Furthermore, movement and non-awakening arise together in conjunction such that they cannot be distinguished;
therefore, at the moment of conception (*tson-shi*), ignorance is not different from the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Moreover, non-awakening itself carries the meaning of delusive darkness.
Because it arises as that which is perfumed by ignorance at the time of its fruition in the past,
it takes that very ignorance at the time of fruition as its cause.
"Movement" (iṅgita) signifies, in itself, the meaning of transformation (vikāra).
Because it arises through being perfumed by false conceptualization (vikalpa),
that very conceptualization serves as its cause. Therefore,
at the stage of the "son" (the resultant state), ignorance (avidyā) and the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna) are not identical.
This means that at the stage of the cause, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the consciousness of karma are neither identical nor different.
As for the fact that at the stage of the fruit, ignorance and delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are neither identical nor different:
ignorance, by its very nature, carries the meaning of non-comprehension.
Because ignorance arises at the hour of the rat,
that very ignorance of the rat-hour serves as the cause.
"Discursive thought" (vikalpa) here carries the meaning of the spontaneous arising of waves of conceptual differentiation.
Because it arises from the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*),
it takes that very karmic consciousness as its cause;
therefore, ignorance and deluded conceptualization are not identical.
Furthermore, because the mental consciousness does not realize that objects are empty,
it gives rise to false conceptualization.
If one realizes their emptiness, false attachment and conceptualization will not arise.
Furthermore, if there is no ignorance, there is no delusive conceptualization;
if there is no delusive conceptualization, there is also no ignorance.
Moreover, these two dharmas arise together in conjunction and cannot be distinguished from one another.
Therefore, they are not different.
This means that at the time of the fruit, ignorance and conceptual construction are neither identical nor different. For this reason:
The two kinds of ignorance constitute the essence;
the deluded thoughts of karmic consciousness constitute the function.
These two kinds of ignorance mutually serve as cause and effect for one another.
Karmic consciousness and deluded thought also serve as cause and effect for one another.
If the seeds and fruits of ignorance act as mutual causes,
this constitutes the condition of direct causality (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That false conceptualization and the karmic consciousness act as mutual causes is also a case of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). If,
at the time of the "son," ignorance gives rise to the karmic consciousness, [it is likewise so].
This is precisely the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, when ignorance gives rise to conceptual construction at the time of the fruit,
this too is the dominant condition.
The preceding section has clarified the empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Next, regarding the clarification of the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha,
there are two types of distinctions within it.
First, it clarifies that [the *ālayavijñāna*] is not empty by demonstrating its possession of both defiled and pure phenomena.
Second, it clarifies the identity and difference of the essence of the *garbha* to explain its substantial existence.
Regarding the first point, the clarification of the two types of phenomena—defiled and pure:
First, the pure dharmas are explained;
next, the defiled dharmas are explained.
First, the pure dharmas are explained.
Within this, there are further two kinds of distinctions:
first, clarifying the possession of the dharmas of untainted (anāsrava) nature and merit;
second, clarifying the possession of the dharmas of purity through the removal of hindrances.
First, regarding the possession of the qualities of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*):
although this pure mind is of a single, equal flavor and its essence is without differentiation,
it nevertheless possesses untainted qualities numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.
That is to say, because its intrinsic nature possesses the meaning of the great radiance of wisdom;
because it possesses the meaning of true and authentic cognition;
and because it possesses the meanings of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Such immeasurable and boundless dharmas of intrinsic purity are possessed solely by the one mind,
as explained in detail in the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.
This pure mind possesses these dharmas of intrinsic purity.
Therefore, it is called "not empty.
Second, regarding the possession of the pure qualities that transcend obstacles:
this refers to the fact that the essence of this pure mind inherently possesses the merit of natural purity.
Therefore, one is able to maintain the power of the habitual perfuming of pure karma; by the power of this perfuming, the functions of virtue manifest.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because of the wisdom-activity of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) on the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
It perfumes the three natures of wisdom, causing their functions to arise and manifest;
these are precisely the three great wisdoms of the Tathāgata’s fruition-virtue.
Furthermore, by means of all modes of practice, such as the five pāramitās of the causal stage, [the fruit is perfected].
The perfuming of the nature of the primary and secondary marks causes their functional manifestation;
this is precisely the retributive fruit of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs.
Nevertheless, although these dharmas of the fruit-virtue possess distinct characteristics, they are nonetheless one in essence.
Yet its essence is the one mind;
because the essence of the mind possesses these virtues, it is called "not empty.
This explains "not empty" in terms of the meaning of the mind's essence itself.
Why is this? Because the essence of the mind is equal, being neither empty nor non-empty. Question:
Regarding that which can perfume pure karma:
does it arise from the mind, or is there a distinct pure dharma external to the mind that acts as the perfumer? Answer:
The dharmas that act as perfumers are all produced by the single mind.
What is the meaning of this?
That is to say, all the teachings one has heard are produced from the minds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
they are the mind of the Buddhas.
Because the bodhisattva-mind and the sentient-being-mind are one,
the teaching does not exist outside the mind.
Furthermore, one uses this teaching to permeate the mind and the nature of understanding.
This nature relies on the permeation of the teaching to give rise to the function of understanding;
therefore, understanding is likewise a product of the mind.
Because the nature of the activity that perfumes the mind is understood through its resolution, and because this nature arises as the functional activity of practice based on that resolving perfume,
such activity is likewise a construction of the mind.
Because the nature of the fruit is perfumed by practice,
and that nature relies upon the perfuming of practice to give rise to the virtues of the fruit,
the fruit, in turn, is produced by this single mind alone.
Speaking from this perspective, the teaching is centered on the single mind,
and even the fruit is centered on the single mind;
there is no other dharma whatsoever.
For this reason, when the substance of the mind exists in the state of ordinary beings,
it inherently possesses the nature of liberation, practice, fruition, and virtue; however,
it has simply not yet been perfumed by the True Suchness and the methods of the Buddhas.
Therefore, understanding and the like have not yet manifested their functioning.
If the nature of understanding and the like did not exist fundamentally,
then even if one were to infuse it with cultivation, its virtuous functioning would ultimately never manifest.
In this way, true gold possesses by its very nature the potential for being a vessel,
and even the subtle excellence required for it to become a finished vessel;
yet, because it has not yet undergone the application of hammering and forging, the utility of the vessel and so forth does not manifest.
Subsequently, by applying tongs, hammers, and tools, the finished vessel gradually manifests.
If the gold itself did not originally possess the nature of becoming a finished vessel from a raw material,
then even if one were to apply effort and labor, [it could never be made].
The employment of the fundamental nature by Puk Yong-sung will ultimately remain unmanifested.
It is like pressing sand to seek oil, drilling ice to find fire, forging ice into vessels, or casting wood to make a jar;
these can never be accomplished because they lack an inherent nature from the very beginning.
Therefore, the treatise states: "If sentient beings lacked the Buddha-nature, even if they were to cultivate the path, they would not attain Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is the essence of the pure mind [that constitutes the Buddha-nature].
This is the nature of the causal practices and resultant virtues that are inherently possessed.
Based upon this nature, the virtues of cause and effect arise.
Therefore, these virtues have the single mind alone as their essence.
Because this single mind is endowed with these pure virtues,
it is therefore termed the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Next, the possession of defiled dharmas is explained.
Within this, there are further two kinds of distinctions:
first, clarifying the fullness of the nature of defilement;
second, clarifying the fullness of the phenomena of defilement.
First, regarding the explanation of being fully endowed with the nature of defilement:
although this mind is equal and free from characteristics,
it nevertheless possesses the nature of all defiled dharmas.
It can give rise to birth and death and can bring about birth and death.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The nature of the mind is one."
How is it that they can produce various karmic fruits?
That is to say, they can produce birth and death.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
That is to say, the Dharmakāya circulating through the five destinies is designated as "sentient beings";
it is that which is capable of producing birth and death.
[The interlocutor] asks:
If the essence of the mind were inherently possessed of a defiled nature,
then it would be impossible to transform the ordinary into the sacred.
The answer is:
If the essence of the mind possessed only the nature of defilement,
it would be impossible to transform the ordinary into the holy;
since it possesses both the natures of defilement and purity, [such transformation is possible].
Why is it that one cannot transform the ordinary person into a sage?
It is asked: What is the function of the ordinary and the sage?
Since they cannot arise simultaneously,
how could the natures of defilement and purity both exist together?
The answer is:
The essence of the mind of each and every sentient being and the essence of the mind of each and every Buddha inherently possess two natures.
Yet there is no mark of differentiation;
it is of a single flavor and equal, unimpaired throughout past and present.
It is only because the defiled karma perfumes the nature that [distinctions arise].
Thus, the characteristics of birth and death become manifest.
Because pure karma perfumes the pure nature,
the function of nirvana appears.
However, when the essence of the mind of each and every sentient being undergoes birth and death based on perfuming,
it does not preclude that this essence possesses the capacity for pure nature; likewise,
when the essence of the mind of each and every Buddha undergoes nirvana based on perfuming.
Yet this does not obstruct the function of the nature of defilement inherent in the essence. For this reason,
every single sentient being and every single Buddha [are identical].
It fully possesses both the nature of defilement and the nature of purity;
within the dharmadhātu, these have never been absent as a matter of natural law.
It is only through the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) that their functional manifestations arise in temporal succession.
Because they do not coexist, the perfuming of defilements ceases;
therefore, it is called the "transformation of the ordinary.
Because pure karma arises, it is said to be the "attainment of sainthood."
However, in the essence of the mind, these two natures truly possess neither formation nor destruction.
Therefore, when speaking in terms of their nature, both defilement and purity are fully present;
yet when discussing them according to the influence of perfuming, ordinary beings and sages do not coexist.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Within the pure Dharma, not a single phenomenon is seen to increase.
This means that it is inherently endowed with essential purity from the beginning, rather than being something newly produced.
Within the dharmas of affliction (*kleśa*), not a single dharma is seen to diminish;
this is because the inherently present nature of defilement is indestructible.
Nevertheless, by virtue of the conditions of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), pure *prajñā* manifests with ever-increasing excellence.
This means that one becomes a sage through the permeation of pure karma;
herein lie the exhaustion of afflictions and delusive thoughts.
This means that one transforms from an ordinary person through the cessation of defiled karma.
Question: Since defiled karma has no beginning and exists fundamentally, by what means can it be extinguished?
Since pure karma does not exist fundamentally, by what means can it be brought forth?
The answer is:
Because one attains the functioning of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all Buddhas and perfumes the mind, pure karma can arise.
Since purity is able to eliminate defilement, defiled karma is thereby extinguished.
Question: Both defiled and pure karmas arise based on the nature of the mind;
can they, in turn, perfuse the mind?
Since both arise based on the nature (dhātu), how can they exclude one another?
The answer is:
although defiled karma arises based on the nature of the mind, [it does not negate its purity].
Yet [impure karma] is always contrary to the mind,
whereas pure karma also arises based on the nature of the mind and is always in accord with it.
Because it opposes existence, it has the sense of cessation and detachment, and thus serves to purify;
because it accords with existence, it has the capacity for mutual support, and thus can eliminate defilement.
It is the inherent nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that it possesses this function of mutual exclusion.
Why should there be any cause for doubt?
It is asked:
Since the essence of the mind is pure by nature and can give rise to pure karma, can that karma in turn perfume the pure nature of the mind?
The nature of defilement within the substance of the mind is capable of giving rise to defiled karma, which in turn can permeate (*vāsanā*) the defiled nature of the mind.
Therefore, it is possible for defiled karma and the pure nature not to permeate one another; thus, their mutual production is said to be contradictory.
If defiled karma and the nature of defilement were to produce and permeate one another, they should be said to be mutually conforming.
If they are mutually conforming,
then they cannot be extinguished.
If defiled karma, although conforming to a defiled nature,
can be extinguished because it is contrary to a pure nature.
Furthermore, although pure karma accords with the nature of purity, it can also be eliminated because it is contrary to the nature of defilement;
for both would be in contradiction to their respective meanings.
Both possess the sense of "separation" (*niḥsaraṇa*). Furthermore, since they both serve the purpose of maintaining purity and eliminating defilement,
they should both be understood as having the sense of "conducive" (*ānulomika*).
Furthermore, they possess the capacity to support one another;
thus, it is possible to preserve the defiled while setting aside the pure. He replied:
My position is not as you have described; why then do you raise this objection?
I say that because pure karma accords with the mind, the pure nature of the mind's essence is itself in accord with its fundamental state.
Because defiled karma opposes the mind, the defiled nature of the mind's essence is itself in opposition to its fundamental state.
If one discusses the essence of the mind exclusively, it is equal toward both the favorable and the adverse;
however, by conforming to its original arising as pure, one conforms to the non-dual essence of the pure mind.
Therefore, there is the capacity for mutual support.
To deviate from the fundamental and give rise to defilement is to contradict the principle of the equality of *tathatā*;
therefore, there is the meaning of cessation and separation.

Question: If one opposes the root, one opposes the branch; if one opposes the branch, one opposes the essence of non-duality. Thus, they should both [be opposed].
There is the meaning of transcendence and cessation.
Why, then, was it stated above that the dharma-realm is naturally endowed with these two natures and is indestructible?
The answer is:
Although that which opposes the root may arise as opposition to the branches,
because it is nonetheless a functional manifestation of principle, it is of one flavor with what is compliant;
thus, it cannot be eliminated.
Although the derivative [nature] depends on the fundamental [nature], it is merely a functional manifestation; thus, it possesses a distinct character and can therefore be extinguished.
By this principle, the meaning that the two natures do not destroy one another is established.
Question: I still do not understand the meaning of "the function of defilement being contrary to the mind.
I pray that you will explain it for me.
The answer is:
The defiled dharma of ignorance truly arises from the defiled nature of the essence of mind.
However, because their substance is obscured,
they do not know that themselves and all objective realms arise from the mind;
nor do they know that the pure mind is fully endowed with both the natures of defilement and purity, yet remains without any marks of difference.
Because one does not understand this principle of uniform equality,
it is termed "contradiction.
The pure dharma of wisdom truly arises from the essence of the mind.
Because of its clarity and sharpness, one is able to know that both oneself and all phenomena are produced from the mind.
Furthermore, one knows that the essence of the mind is fully endowed with the two natures of defilement and purity, yet remains without any marks of differentiation.
One knows this in accordance with reason through the equality of the single flavor;
therefore, it is called "conformity.
It is like a destitute son who is actually born of his father, and whom the father truly cherishes and remembers.
It is only because of delusion that he does not know he was born from his father,
nor does he understand his father's intentions;
though he dwells in his father’s house, he does not recognize him as his father.
This was called a transgression.
Furthermore, his father enticed and instructed him for many years until he finally realized that he had been born from his father.
Furthermore, he understood his father’s intention;
he then took charge of the family estate and received his father’s instructions,
and was named Shun.
Sentient beings are likewise;
because of ignorance,
they do not know that their own bodies and all phenomena arise entirely from the mind.
Furthermore, by encountering the skillful means and teachings of the Buddhas,
one follows and accords with the pure mind and is thus able to realize True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is asked:
Since it has been stated that the defiled dharma of ignorance is contrary to the mind,
how can it permeate the mind?
The answer is:
Because the defiled phenomena of ignorance have no separate substantial entity, they are not distinct from the pure mind;
and because they are not distinct from the mind, although they are mutually contradictory, they are able to mutually permeate one another.
Just as fire produced from wood blazes up, rising in opposition to the very substance of the wood,
yet because it has no separate essence and is not distinct from the wood, it returns to burn that same wood; later,
if one does not hear this analogy, one will instead give rise to the misconception that [the mind] is like a lamp or a furnace.
This clarifies that the essence of the mind is fully endowed with the nature of defilement, which is termed "not empty.
Next, it clarifies that the essence of the mind is fully endowed with the phenomena of defilement;
that is, that very nature of defilement is perfumed by the karma of defilement.
Thus, it constitutes the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) and the seeds of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).
Based upon these seeds, various karmic fruits and retributions (*vipāka*) manifest.
This ignorance, as well as karma and its fruit, constitute the defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśavastu*).
Nevertheless, although these— the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), seeds, and the retribution of fruits—
manifest with distinct characteristics, they are described as "phenomena."
Yet all [phenomena] have the single mind as their essence and do not exist outside of the mind.
For this reason, this mind is further regarded as non-empty.
It is, for example, like the forms and images manifested by a clear mirror, which have no separate essence of their own.
It is but a single mirror, yet it does not obstruct the distinct differentiation of myriad images;
the various states of this difference all manifest within the mirror.
Therefore, it is called the "Mirror of Non-Emptiness."
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* speaks of the "mirror of perfuming," which refers to that which is truly non-empty,
wherein all worldly realms appear.
All these appear therein,
neither emerging nor entering, neither losing nor perishing,
eternally abiding within a single mind.
Because all phenomena are themselves the nature of reality;
verified by this, they are fully endowed with the defiled phenomena of the world.
This is also the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus far, it has been clarified that it is fully endowed with both defiled and pure dharmas;
this concludes the explanation of the meaning of "non-emptiness."

Fifth, it clarifies the meaning of how the reception of retribution differs according to delusion.
Sixth, it clarifies common and uncommon consciousnesses.
