Question: Regarding the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha,
does each and every sentient being possess their own individual Tathāgatagarbha?
Do all sentient beings and all buddhas share only a single tathāgatagarbha?
The answer is:
All sentient beings and all buddhas [share it].
It is solely the one *tathāgatagarbha* shared [by all].
It is asked: "Regarding that which is called the essence of the *garbha*, how does it encompass both the defiled and the pure?"
Is it possessed [of both] simultaneously, or is it possessed from beginning to end?
The answer is:
when it is said that the Tathāgatagarbha possesses both the defiled and the pure, [it refers to its possession from beginning to end].
There are two kinds:
first, defilement of nature and purity of nature;
second, defilement of phenomena and purity of phenomena.
This has already been clarified above.
If one relies on the perspective of the defilement and purity of nature (*svabhāva*), then both have coexisted since time immemorial.
If one relies on the perspective of the defilement and purity of phenomena (*vastu*), then there are two kinds of distinctions.
First, that within each single moment both defilement and purity are simultaneously present;
second, that defilement and purity are present only from beginning to end.
What is the meaning of this?
This means that the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with the nature of all sentient beings,
each of which is distinct and different;
this is precisely the differentiation within non-differentiation.
Furthermore, within the nature of each and every sentient being,
there has been from the very beginning the possession of immeasurable and boundless natures;
namely, the six realms and the four modes of birth.
Suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness,
lifespan and physical stature,
folly and wisdom, and so forth.
All worldly defiled phenomena,
as well as the causes and fruits of the three vehicles,
and all supramundane pure phenomena.
Such immeasurable varieties of dharma-nature are fully present,
without exception, within the nature of each and every sentient being.
For this reason, the Tathāgatagarbha has from the very beginning possessed both the defiled and pure natures simultaneously.
Because it possesses the defiled nature, it is able to manifest all the defiled phenomena of sentient beings.
Therefore, this treasury is taken as the dharmakāya abiding primordially within the state of obstruction;
it is also called buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). Furthermore, because it is endowed with the nature of purity, it is able to manifest all the pure virtues equal to those of all Buddhas.
Therefore, this treasury is taken as the Dharma-body that has emerged from obstructions;
it is also called the Dharma-body of innate purity,
and it is also called the nirvana of innate purity.
Nevertheless, although each and every sentient being has,
since beginningless time, been endowed with both the defiled and pure natures,
this is due solely to the differences in the karma they have created.
The nature of the perfumed seeds constitutes their function as seeds;
furthermore, because there are distinct functions for these distinct seeds,
the retributions experienced within a single moment differ accordingly.
That is to say, there are those who attain Buddhahood;
those who realize the fruits of the Two Vehicles;
and those who enter the three miserable realms.
There are those born among gods and humans;
furthermore, within each of these realms of rebirth, there are immeasurable distinctions and differences. Judging by this:
Within the Tathāgatagarbha-mind,
both defiled and pure phenomena are simultaneously and fully present;
as it is at one moment, so it is at all times.
Nevertheless, although each of these ordinary beings and sages receives their respective retributions at a particular time,
the phenomena of causes and conditions are not fixed.
Every ordinary being and sage, since beginningless time, has passed through all realms of existence, undergoing countless cycles of rebirth;

subsequently, they encounter virtuous friends who instruct them in the practice of renunciation, lead them to train in the paths of the Three Vehicles, and enable them to attain the fruits of the Way.
According to this treatise, every single sentient being possesses both defiled and pure aspects from beginning to end.
Why is this? Because when a single sentient being receives a body in the hells, there is no karmic retribution remaining for other realms of existence.
When experiencing the retribution of the heavenly realms, there is no retribution for other destinies;
when experiencing each individual body within each individual destiny, there is likewise no retribution for other bodies.
Furthermore, while experiencing worldly retribution, one cannot attain supramundane fruits.
When one experiences supramundane fruits, there is no mundane retribution. For this reason,
a single sentient being cannot simultaneously possess both defiled and pure states.
From beginning to end, it possesses both matters.
All sentient beings are likewise.
Therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha has the meaning of possessing both defiled and pure matters from beginning to end.
Question: When the Tathāgatagarbha is endowed with such immeasurable dharmatās as these,
is there differentiation or is there no differentiation?
The answer is:
The essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* is equal and truly without distinction;
this is precisely the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Furthermore, this essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses inconceivable functions;
thus, its being fully endowed with all dharma-natures in their distinct particularities constitutes the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
This is indeed the differentiation within non-differentiation.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that it is not like a lump of clay, which possesses a multitude of atoms.
Why is this? A lump of clay is provisional, whereas atoms are real;
therefore, each individual atom possesses its own distinct substance.
It is merely through combination that they form a single lump of clay;
this lump of clay possesses the distinctions of many particles.
The Tathāgatagarbha is not like this.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgatagarbha is the true Dharma, perfectly interfused and non-dual.
Therefore, the entire essence of the Tathāgata-garbha is identical to the nature of a single pore of a single sentient being.
The entire body is the nature of every single pore of a sentient being.
Just as it is with the nature of the pores,
so too is the nature of each and every phenomenon within all other worlds.
Just as the mundane dharmic nature of a single sentient being is so,
the mundane dharmic nature of every single sentient being is likewise;
and the supramundane dharmic nature of every single Buddha is also thus.
This is the totality of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, by taking up the nature of a single sentient being’s single pore,
one encompasses the worldly dharma-nature possessed by all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it encompasses all the supramundane dharmic natures of all Buddhas.
Just as raising the nature of a single pore encompasses the natures of all phenomena,
so too is it with every other individual mundane dharma-nature.
Just as one encompasses the nature of every single phenomenon in the world,
so too does one encompass the nature of all phenomena; likewise, it is the same for every single phenomenon belonging to the supramundane.
This immediately encompasses the nature of all phenomena.
Furthermore, just as the matter of raising a single pore encompasses all mundane and supramundane matters, so it is here.
Just as mentioning the matter of a single pore encompasses all matters,
so it is likewise for every single thing among all that exists within the mundane and supramundane realms.
This encompasses all mundane and supramundane matters. Why is this?
Because it includes all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Because it takes that very nature of the mundane and the supramundane as its essence,
the essences of the mundane and the supramundane are thus fused and mutually inclusive; therefore,
mundane and supramundane phenomena [are likewise so].
This is precisely the state of perfect interfusion, mutual inclusion, and non-obstruction.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
It is like a bright mirror whose substance possesses the nature of all images, yet each image is distinct and different from the others.
This is precisely the differentiation within non-differentiation.
If this mirror-substance fundamentally lacked the principle of differentiation regarding the nature of images,
then even if various forms were brought before it, images would never appear.
Just as that blazing fire, though bright and pure, cannot manifest images because it fundamentally lacks the nature of images,
yet one sees that a mirror can manifest images.
One knows with certainty that the nature of images is inherently present; for this reason,
within a single moment, this one bright mirror—
Both are able to manifest all images, whether pure or defiled;
yet the pure image does not obstruct the defiled,
nor does the defiled image obstruct the pure.
There is no obstruction or hindrance, yet there is a distinction between purity and impurity based on function.
Nevertheless, although there is this distinction between the essence of the image and the characteristics of the image,
they are further perfectly interfused and not different.
It is solely a single mirror.
Why is this? Because this mirror, in its entirety, is of the same nature as the image within a single pore.
The whole is the nature of the images within all pores; just as it is with the nature of the images within the pores,

The nature of the image is uniformly pure; the nature of the image is uniformly defiled.
The nature of the image is likewise so.
This is the entire substance of the mirror.
Therefore, if one raises the nature of the image of a single pore,
it encompasses all other natures of images;
just as when the nature of the image of a single pore is raised.
This encompasses all image-natures.
To take each of the remaining individual image-natures one by one, it is likewise so;
that is, they encompass all image-natures.
Furthermore, if one raises the image-form of a single pore, it encompasses all image-forms;
just as raising the image-form of a single pore encompasses all image-forms,
so too is it for each and every other image-form that is raised.
This immediately encompasses all image-aspects. Why?
Because all image-aspects have that very nature of images as their essence.
Therefore, the nature and substance of all images are fused and mutually inclusive;
thus, the characteristics of all images are likewise fused and mutually inclusive.
By means of this analogy:
One should believe that all Buddhas and all sentient beings are of one and the same pure mind— the Tathāgatagarbha— and that they do not obstruct one another.
Therefore, the sūtra says:
"It is like a bright, clear mirror in which the images of faces appear according to their presence;

The nature of karma is also like this.

It refers to a bright and clear mirror.

Therefore, it is able to receive all perfumations;
according to the distinctions among those perfumations, the retributions manifested differ.

"Nature" refers to...

Now, it is not at all contradictory that the Universal Radiance can produce both mundane and supramundane fruits;
therefore, the Treatise says:
"The third is the Greatness of Function."
Because it can give rise to the causes and effects of good and evil in both the mundane and supramundane realms, for this reason,
the minds of all ordinary beings and sages have a single mind as their essence.
This is certain and beyond doubt.
Furthermore, the sutra states:
"The dharma-body of all Buddhas..."
The phrase "it is solely this single Dharma-body" means that it is realized and known that all Buddhas have the same true mind as their essence,
because the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are one.
All sentient beings and all Buddhas are of one and the same Dharma-body.
Why is this? Because the Sūtras serve as proof.
What is that which is realized?
It is said that this very dharmakāya, when it flows through the five destinies, is called a sentient being;
when it reverses its flow and exhausts its source, it is called a Buddha.
For this reason,
all sentient beings and all Buddhas share only one single pure mind.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the equal Dharmakāya.

neither one nor different;

therefore, it is called "mind.

thus, the distinct dharmakāyas of each individual on the path and each individual among ordinary beings and sages are likewise not lost.
Why is this? Because it is based on the meaning of the distinction between genders.
[The questioner] asks:

The answer is:

it is not a nature formed through habituation.

if one says that the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha possesses the nature of defilement and is capable of producing birth and death;

other cases may be understood by analogy with this. For this reason:
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha can give rise to birth and death;
this does not contradict the principle that the Buddha-nature exists within the bodies of all sentient beings. Question:
If True Suchness (tathatā) is called "nirvana of intrinsic purity" when it is free from obstructions,
then when True Suchness is within obstructions, it should be called "birth-and-death of intrinsic defilement. How, then, can it be termed "Buddha-nature"?
The answer is:
Although the reality that remains within the fetters possesses a nature of defilement in its essence,
it is therefore able to establish the function of birth and death.
Because the essence itself is endowed with the nature of purity,
it possesses the ultimate capacity to emerge from obstructions;
therefore, it is called Buddha-nature.

then regardless of whether it is in a state of obstruction or free from obstruction,

Question: Since all ordinary beings and sages have this single mind as their essence,

There are those who share in enjoyment and those who do not share in enjoyment.
The answer is:
as for the statement that all ordinary beings and sages have nothing but the single mind as their essence—
If this mind is discussed in terms of its essence and characteristics, there are two kinds.
The first is the mind of the equality of True Suchness; this is the essence.
This is precisely the Dharmakāya, the common characteristic shared equally by all ordinary beings and sages.
Second, the ālayavijñāna is itself the characteristic.
Within this ālayavijñāna, there are further two kinds.
The first is the dependent nature of the pure portion,
also called the consciousness of pure synthesis;
it is the very essence of all noble beings.
The second is the dependent nature as the basis for defilement,
also called the consciousness of defiled conjunction;
it is the very essence of all sentient beings.
Although these two types of dependent nature differ in their functional applications,
their essence is harmoniously fused into a single flavor;
it is nothing other than the single, true suchness, the mind of equality.
Because these two types of dependent nature are identical in essence and non-dual,
there are nevertheless two distinct matters within them.
The first is the consciousness of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*).
Second, there are non-common consciousnesses. Why do they exist?
Because within the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), both the nature of common consciousness and the nature of non-common consciousness are fully present.
Because all ordinary beings and sages create identical karma that perfumes this common characteristic (sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa),
it constitutes the common-characteristic consciousness (sādhāraṇa-vijñāna).
If each ordinary being and sage were to individually create their own distinct karma, [it would not be so].
Because this uncommon nature is perfumed,
it becomes the uncommon consciousness. Why is this so?
That which is called "external dharmas," such as the five sense objects and the receptacle world,
which are experienced in common by all ordinary beings and sages,
is the characteristic of the shared-aspect consciousness (*sādhāraṇa-vijñapti-lakṣaṇa*).
Just as all sentient beings who collectively cultivate the practice of Amitāyus all infuse their true mind and its shared nature; this nature,
arising through such infusion, manifests as the Pure Land.
Therefore, both ordinary beings and sages may enjoy [the land] together.
Just as the Pure Land is formed by collective karma,
so too are the other lands of various defilements and impurities.
However, this soil shared by all is merely a manifestation of the mind; therefore,
it is called the "common-characteristic consciousness."
Furthermore, although this shared environment arises from the collective karma of all ordinary beings and sages,
it does not preclude each individual sentient being and each individual sage from creating their own karma within a single lifetime.

Thus, one is able to uniquely evoke this land; for this reason, although immeasurable sentient beings take rebirth in other places, they do not abandon this land, which remains eternally present and never deficient.
Furthermore, although each individual—whether ordinary being or sage—possesses karma that uniquely evokes this land, [the land itself remains constant].
Yet they do not obstruct one another, for there is only a single land.
Therefore, while immeasurable sentient beings are newly born,
the characteristics of the original land remain as they were.
There is no further modification or increase,
except that at that time,
the lands transformed by the superior collective karma of all sentient beings undergoes change.
If the lands transformed by common karma were also subject to change, then they would not be constant; however, if this were not the case, the lands would remain eternally fixed.
That which is called the "unshared characteristic" refers to the distinct retributions within the individual bodies of each ordinary person and sage.
Because the karma created by each individual— whether ordinary person or sage— is distinct, it perfumes the true mind.
This non-common nature of the true mind,
arising in dependence upon such perfuming, manifests as distinct retributions that differ for each person, such that self and other are separate.
However, these distinct retributions are solely mental characteristics;
therefore, they are called "unshared consciousnesses.
Within the category of shared characteristics, there is further the sense of "unshared consciousness."
This means that, for example, hungry ghosts and others have created common karma together with humans;
therefore, they equally receive the retribution of the physical world (bhājana-loka) and can see the Ganges River from afar.
This is because it is a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because their respective karmas (*karma-vipāka*) are particularly heavy, they serve as an obstacle;
thus, when they reach the riverbank, they see only various distinct things and cannot obtain water to drink.
This refers to that which is uncommon within the common.
Furthermore, based on the fact that those of similar kind collectively created the karma for hunger,
they likewise find themselves unable to obtain water to drink upon the banks of the Ganges.
Furthermore, this is the meaning of shared characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Within this, moreover, there are differing perceptions:
some see it as a flowing flame.
Some see it as parched;
some see it as pus, blood, and so forth—there are immeasurable such variations.
Furthermore, these are both common and uncommon [perceptions].
When it manifests in this manner,
that which is perceived and utilized in common by others is termed the "common-characteristic consciousness" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna).
"Different seeing and hearing, different experiencing" refers to the common and uncommon aspects of consciousness,
which are distinguished according to their respective meanings.
All sentient beings can be known to be exactly like this.
Within the context of unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), there is further the sense of commonality (*sādhāraṇa-artha*),
namely, one's retinue and acquaintances.
Even down to those who look upon one another, who share the same environment, the same speech, the same knowledge,
and the same understanding; or those encountered for a moment,
whether they be enemies or kin, as well as neutral persons, whether acquainted or unacquainted.
As for the fact that beings even down to the animal and heavenly realms perceive and recognize one another,
this is entirely due to the nature of their mutual conditioning by past karma— such as the karma of seeing and recognizing— which has perfumed the mind; thus,
it manifests through the power of mental conditioning.
Such matters as seeing and knowing one another are precisely the meaning of the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) within the uncommon characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṇa*). Alternatively,
there may be cases where "I" know and see another, while that other does not know or see me.
Thus, it is common to oneself but uncommon to others;
one may understand the distinctions accordingly according to their meaning.
Furthermore, just as a single person's body is their own unique (asādhāraṇa) object of cognition,
it also serves as the shared (sādhāraṇa) object of cognition for the eighty thousand families of worms that inhabit it;
thus, this very same body is both their common object of cognition and their own.
This is also the meaning of the "common characteristic within the uncommon.
Because of this principle of common and uncommon characteristics,
although all ordinary beings and sages share the same mind as their essence, [they remain distinct].
Thus, there are instances of seeing and not seeing forms, as well as shared and unshared enjoyment.
For this reason, while Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa constantly shines, the trees within the forest remain hidden from its brilliance;
and the sixteen-foot golden body is seen again as earth, ash, and various other colors.
To regard the wondrous realm of the Lotus as a desolate wasteland,
and to mischaracterize the ground adorned with jewels as mere sand and gravel—
all such views arise from the distinction between the common and the uncommon.
This concludes the explanation of the sixfold distinctions regarding the identity and difference of the essence within the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.

when one touches the current, one touches the water.

The mental consciousness has no substance;

Therefore, it is simply that the mental consciousness ceases by itself; it is not that the mental consciousness is able to realize the pure mind.
Therefore, it is said:
as for "the mind being self-attested," when the mental consciousness knows that the fundamental realization (mūla-sākṣātkriyā) knows [itself], it perceives the pure mind.
Thus, one knows that the fundamental realization is the knowing that realizes, while not perceiving the pure mind.
If you say that one who does not perceive a pure mind can nonetheless know and realize [the truth],
then one who does not perceive the Buddha-mind should likewise be able to know and realize the Buddha's realization. If,
however, it is by perceiving a pure mind that one knows and realizes it, then...
The pure mind is itself a visible characteristic.
How can the treatise state that the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind is free from the characteristics of mental objects?
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
It cannot be cognized by consciousness, nor is it the domain of the mind.
By this evidence, one certainly knows that the mental consciousness does not perceive the mind.
Because there is no rational basis for knowing that the mind is fundamentally quiescent through either seeing or not seeing,
even if the essence of the mind were fundamentally realized, the mind of deluded thought could not be stilled.
If it is argued that although false consciousness does not perceive the pure mind,
one can know it because the mind is fundamentally quiescent according to the scriptural teachings,
and thus wisdom perfumes the pure mind, causing the mind to spontaneously realize its own original realization.
The non-arising of subsequent thoughts is what is called self-realization.
When you rely on the scriptural teachings to know that the mind is fundamentally quiescent,
do you know it by constructing a mark of quiescence?
It is known by not forming the mark of tranquility.
If it were known by forming the mark of tranquility,
how could the mark of false conceptualization be called tranquil?
If one does not form a mental image (*nimitta*), the mind will have nothing to which it is bound and will consequently wander and disperse.
If one says that by applying attention (*manasikāra*) one prevents such wandering,
then there is an object of focus (*ālambana*).
Since there is an object of perception, there must still be characteristics;
how then can it be said that one does not produce characteristics?
If you say that the seven consciousnesses are able to perceive the pure mind, [this is likewise untenable].
Therefore, one knows that the mind is fundamentally quiescent.
Having known this, one perfumes the mind so that the mind itself realizes its own fundamental realization; thus, subsequent thoughts do not arise.
To claim that this is what is called "self-realization" is also incorrect. Why?
Because the seven consciousnesses are the consciousnesses of self-clinging.
One cannot perceive that the mind is fundamentally quiescent.
Furthermore, if it were to become an object of the perceiving subject,
it would not be the pure mind.
As has already been explained in the section on the nature and characteristics of the mental substance (*citta*),
since the objects of perception are not real,
the perfuming of the mind gives rise in turn to deluded thoughts.
For this reason, it is illogical that the pure mind,
through self-realization, would not give rise to a subsequent thought.
If one were to say that it is realized by means of another, [it would be untenable].
This is also not so. Why? Because the essence of the mind is inherently quiescent.
It is simply because the six and seventh consciousnesses and so forth are designated as "other" that,
due to the existence of this "other," it is said that the mind of another is not directly realized.
Therefore, it is possible to realize the other.
Why is it necessary to use something else to verify the mind?
If one says that although the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent,
it is merely because it has been perfumed by beginningless ignorance and deluded thoughts.
Because these habitual tendencies of deluded thoughts reside within the mind,
the essence of the mind likewise does not realize quiescence;
therefore, it must be realized by another.
What skillful means can eliminate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the mind so that the mind may realize [the truth]?
If one says that new thoughts do not arise again,
and therefore no longer perfuse and increase those habitual tendencies;
Regarding the statement that "it ceases of its own accord":
while it has not yet ceased, for what reason would a new thought not arise?
This would be the case if there were no distinct factor acting as an antidote.
One should bring to mind those various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
if one brings them to mind, it further increases their power. For this reason:
It is also illogical for it to be realized by another.

If you say that there is no need to employ a mind realized by another, but rather realize the other [object] directly, such that through the realization of the other, one's own habitual tendencies are extinguished; [this is not so].
This is also not the case;
since they have habitual tendencies as their root,
they arise constantly in every moment of thought.
If those seeds of habitual tendencies are not first eliminated,
by what means could false thoughts be realized?
Furthermore, there is no logical principle by which a pure mind could realize another.
If one were able to realize this in others,
then all sentient beings would possess a pure mind,
and their deluded thoughts would naturally be eliminated in their entirety.
If it is said that deluded thoughts mutually suppress one another before and after,

and thus cease after a long time, and are therefore called "realizing the other," then does the former suppress the latter or the latter suppress the former? If you say that the preceding thought suppresses the succeeding thought:

When the former exists, the latter consciousness has not yet arisen; when the latter arises, the former thought-moment has already passed away. Since they do not reach one another, how can the latter stop the former?
If you say that the latter thought-moment stops the former, [this is untenable].
It is likewise thus that they do not pursue one another;
how then can they be stilled?
If, at the very moment a preceding thought arises, one immediately regrets its arising.
If the mind that gives rise to aversion perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to prevent subsequent moments of thought from arising,
then since the mind does not perceive itself,
how can it feel aversion toward itself?
If a subsequent thought detests a preceding one,
and this detesting mind perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) so that the preceding thought does not arise again,
then when this detesting mind detests the preceding mind, it must do so because it knows the preceding mind to be empty.
One feels aversion because one does not know this emptiness;
if one knows it as emptiness, that is precisely the wisdom of the absence of objects (*anārambaṇajñāna*).
Why do you say that this wisdom is unnecessary?
Furthermore, if one knows this to be empty, one should not harbor aversion toward it.
If one does not know that the preceding thought is empty,
this mind is precisely ignorance.
Why is this? Because they cannot know that the preceding thought is truly empty,
and furthermore, they do not know that the preceding thought is empty.
To harbor the notion that things possess substantial reality and thereby give rise to aversion is precisely deluded thought. Why is this?
Because one falsely conceives of what is empty as being substantially real.
Since this mind that is capable of aversion is itself ignorance and delusive conceptualization, it is a phenomenon of movement;
yet you further say it "perfumes the mind.
This merely increases one's lack of awakening.
Furthermore, it repeatedly increases the consciousness that arises through movement;
thus, to claim that one can prevent subsequent moments of thought from arising is surely a dream within a dream, for one has not yet awakened.
Therefore, this statement is made as if one were not asleep;
otherwise, one certainly would not speak in such a manner.
Furthermore, if it is said that mindfulness does not arise because one does not form mental conceptions regarding all phenomena, [then...]
One does not form mental conceptions regarding the pure mind;
one does not form mental conceptions regarding this mental consciousness.
If it is the pure mind that does not form mental conceptions, [then...]
Originally, for what reason did you give rise to the thought of the Dharma?
Now, for what reason do you suddenly not contemplate the Dharma?
If it is the mental consciousness that does not contemplate the Dharma, [then...]
Mental consciousness is precisely that which is mindful.
If one were to say that mental consciousness does not form mental impressions regarding phenomena,
it would mean that it does not attend to them when confronted with the objects of the mind.
Is it because one does not face the mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*) that one does not attend to them?
Or is it because one faces them but does not see them that one does not attend to them?
Or is it called "non-attention" because one does not face the objects at all?
If it does not encounter an object, how can it be called "mental consciousness"? Why?
Because that which is consciousness must cognize an object of cognition.
If one faces [an object] yet does not see it, this is the dharma of the stubbornly blind.
If one sees yet does not contemplate, for what reason is there no contemplation?
It is because one knows emptiness that one therefore does not contemplate.
It means that because things exist, one does not dwell on them.
If one knows them to be empty— that is, the wisdom that perceives the absence of objective dust—
one confronts them but does not see them, and seeing them, one does not dwell on them.
There is no contradiction in either case.
Why do you say that this wisdom is unnecessary?
If you claim it exists, then one cannot avoid being mindful of it.
Furthermore, they claim that when something exists, it is already a thought; yet, because they claim it exists,
they fail to realize that this is merely the deluded conceptualization of ignorance and thus do not reflect upon it.
For example, when a timid person enters a dark place, the correct way is to enter with eyes open;
yet, being deluded by the external darkness, they become terrified and enter with eyes closed.
With both the inside and outside in darkness, they instead claim it is secure.
This is also like that:
when recollecting a previous phenomenon, it arises solely from the ignorance that deludes the object;
when one does not recollect with a mind of aversion, both the mind and its object are darkened.
On the contrary, they call this "skillful.
Furthermore, if one does not apply attention to mental phenomena (*dharma*), the mind will wander and scatter;
yet if one applies attention while not being mindful of all phenomena, [the same occurs].
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is itself a state of agitation and movement, not a state of tranquility;
how, then, can it be called "realizing the mind"?
It is simply because one focuses the mind exclusively on this [object] and does not think of anything else.
One takes this very non-thought as the object;
because the mental consciousness is bound to this object,
there is no possibility for it to apprehend other objects.
Therefore, those who are deluded do not understand this matter;
they claim that there is no further objective support (*ālambana*) regarding all phenomena,
and consequently, they develop an even deeper attachment to it, regarding it as the true Dharma.
Therefore, the intention of the application continues without ceasing;
because it has been practiced for a long time day and night,
it proceeds spontaneously without the need for deliberate mental effort.
Yet they do not realize that birth and death flow incessantly and arise at every moment;
nor do they know, as they arise, that their ignorance and delusive thoughts have not been dispelled by even a hair’s breadth.
Furthermore, they do not understand what stage of existence their own bodies occupy.
To then say, "My mind abides in tranquility;
this must be the samādhi of True Suchness"—
to harbor such a calculation is perhaps acceptable, yet it reveals a lack of discernment regarding one's own capacity.
Nevertheless, because it consists of single-minded concentration on a single object,
it is also a method of *śamatha* (calm abiding) that serves as a foundation for the wisdom free from dust (*vimalajñāna*) in the distant future.
Compared to being shackled by the restlessness of a monkey,
and contrasted with those who cling to the five desires and sport with the six sense-faculties,
this [state] is hundreds of thousands of millions of times more distinguished and superior.
It is merely the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā), which is the tranquil illumination of the essence of mind.
Therefore, for a practitioner to act without attachment is the gradual dharma-gate.
If one wishes to accomplish the supramundane path, one must necessarily rely upon wisdom free from dust.
This concludes the section on the basis for the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā, specifically answering the question of what that basis is.
This marks the end of the first of the five points established at the outset.
Next, the objective domain of śamatha and vipaśyanā is explained; this refers to the phenomena of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
Within this, there is further a twofold distinction:
first, a general explanation of the three natures;
second, a specific explanation of the three natures.
Regarding the statement that this collectively clarifies the three natures:
that which is True Suchness free from obstructions and the pure virtues of a Buddha are both termed the "nature of reality" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
That True Suchness while still under obstruction, conjoined with defilement, is termed the *ālayavijñāna*.

This refers to the fact that, based on the nature of the stages (bhūmi), the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness—all their deluded conceptualizations and discriminations—are termed the "nature of discrimination" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
This is the teaching concerning the general framework.
As for what is called the "specific clarification of the three natures":
First, the true nature (*tathatā*) is analyzed.
Within this, there are two kinds: first, the defiled pure mind as the true nature;
second, the undefiled pure mind as the true nature.
What is called the "defiled and pure mind" is the actual substance of sentient beings, the fundamental nature of defilement,
which fully possesses the function of opposition and manifests through the transformation of habitual perfuming.
Therefore, it is said to be "with defilement.
Yet its essence encompasses purity and its self-nature is untainted;
the defilements that act as perfumers are fundamentally empty.
The manifestations that appear are eternally quiescent and are further termed "pure"; therefore,
it is said that there is a mind both defiled and pure.
That which is called the "stainless pure mind" is the essential nature of all Buddhas and the fundamental reality of their pure virtues;
although it possesses a nature of spontaneous, contrary functions.
As the perfuming of defilement ceases, defilement is forever extinguished;
furthermore, it is endowed with the capacity for the spontaneous functioning of its own nature.
As the perfuming of purity becomes full, the qualities of purity are manifested.
Therefore, it is called "stainless.
Although it is manifested through perfuming,
the function of its intrinsically pure nature does not increase.
When the obscuring clouds are dispelled,
the power of the essence’s illumination is inherently present;
thus, it is further termed "pure."
Therefore, it is said that the mind is pure and stainless;
yet, depending on its conditioning and in terms of its functional application,
there is the distinction between being stained and being stainless.
Speaking of the essence in terms of its reality,
there is fundamentally no distinction between being unstained and being stained;
this is precisely the equal, true nature.
This is the Great Universal Dharma-gate;
therefore, it is called "the nature of reality" (*tathatā*). Question:
Since it has already been stated that there is both defilement and purity, one should also refer to it as being "without defilement.
The answer is:
This meaning is also present:
the divergent functions of the Buddhas are themselves free from defilement;
it is merely for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon defilement and aspire toward purity.
Therefore, it is not made manifest.
Second, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) also has two types:
first, the pure portion of the dependent nature.
The second is the dependent nature as the defiled portion.
The dependent nature as the purified portion is the very essence of that suchness.
It possesses the functional capacity for both defiled and pure natures;
however, once it is perfumed solely by untainted pure dharmas,
its function regarding defilement is completely exhausted.
It is called "purity.
Furthermore, because it is permeated by that pure karma,
the function of its intrinsically pure nature manifests.
Therefore, it is called "dependent" (paratantra).
That which is manifested is precisely the three bodies (trikāya) and pure lands that are realized;
it consists of all virtues for one's own benefit and the benefit of others.
Question: What is meant by the statement that the functioning of the nature’s defilement does not give rise to birth and death because it is extinguished through the permeation of purification?
Nevertheless, after attaining Buddhahood, does this nature have no function at all?
The answer is:
Although this nature does not give rise to birth and death because it has been permeated by the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is nevertheless due to the fact that [the practitioner] has,
since first generating the resolve for enlightenment, [cultivated the path].
Due to the permeation of the power of compassionate vows,
and for the sake of those with the capacity to be transformed, the function of manifesting apparent opposition through the conditions of permeation is also revealed.

This refers to manifesting identity with the six realms of existence, demonstrating the presence of the three poisons, and expediently undergoing the retribution of suffering, such as following death and extinction.
This refers to the dharma of the pure aspect of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
A question is asked:
"Since it arises from the defiled nature, why is it called the 'pure aspect'?"
Answer: It is solely because of these Buddha-virtues;
it is because of the Buddha in relation to sentient beings.
This quality is designated as "pure.
If one were to discuss defilement and purity solely from the perspective of the Buddha's qualities,
this quality would in fact be a manifestation of a function that appears contrary to defilement.
Question: Since you have already spoken of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature),
why is it called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature)?
The answer is:
Because this virtue arises through being permeated by compassion and vows,
it is a phenomenon of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If these virtues are applied toward conditioned phenomena as objects of perception,
they are termed dharmas of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Question:
If the stainless true nature (*amala-tathatā*) and the purified dependent nature (*viśuddha-paratantra-svabhāva*) are thus [described], what difference is there between them?
The answer is:
The nature of stainless reality (vimalatathatā) has the meaning of its essence being manifest as free from obstructions;
this is precisely its essence.
As for the pure dependent nature (viśuddhaparatantrasvabhāva):
That which arises as a manifest phenomenon through the power of habitual perfuming, characterized by the differentiation of pure qualities,
is precisely the "characteristic" (nimitta).
This refers to the purified nature of parikalpita-svabhāva.
To designate [the object] as a condition is itself the capacity,
which is precisely its function.
As for what is called the "defiled dependent nature":
Although that pure mind inherently possesses the nature of both the adverse and the favorable functions,
it is nevertheless perfumed by the defiled dharmas of ignorance existing within the nature of discrimination.
Its nature is contrary [to purity], functioning through the manifestation of illusory states based on perfuming and transformation;
that is to say, it revolves through birth and death within the six destinies.
Therefore, it is called the defiled *paratantra-svabhāva*.
Question: Because the function of the nature's compliance has not yet been permeated by pure karma,
it cannot manifest.
Although it exists within the cycle of birth and death, is it not entirely without utility?
The answer is:
although it has not yet been permeated by the untainted (*anāsrava*), its pure qualities do not manifest.
However, because they are protected and sustained by the power of the Buddhas’ wisdom of the same essence,
they cultivate the virtues of humans and devas, encounter spiritual friends, and gradually give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment;
this is precisely the functioning of the intrinsically pure nature.
Question: Since all sentient beings equally possess the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and are protected by all Buddhas,
for what reason do they differ in the sequence of their resolve, such that some generate the aspiration [for enlightenment] while others do not?
The answer is:
Since beginningless time, there have been differences in the karma created;
their lightness or heaviness is not uniform, and their sequence is not fixed.
Those whose karmic defilements are light receive the power of the Buddha’s wisdom;
those whose karmic defilements are heavy do not receive it despite having such power.
A question is asked:
If one's defilements and stains are heavy, does the functional capacity of the intrinsically pure nature lack any power at all?
The answer is:
there is simply the substance of intrinsic purity that remains unimpaired.
Because the defilements are heavy, there is no further capacity [to manifest].
A question is asked:
It was stated above that the essence of both ordinary beings and sages possesses both the nature of compliance and the nature of opposition.
It is solely due to the power of defiled and pure perfuming that [the seeds] appear or do not appear.
Why is it that while the Buddhas possess the fulfillment of pure perfuming, they are nonetheless able to manifest functions that appear contrary [to their nature] with great power,
whereas ordinary beings, whose defiled karma is even more heavy, are rendered entirely incapable of making their fundamental nature accordant with its function?
If it is argued that because defilement is heavy, the nature lacks the capacity for purity,
then it should also follow that because purity is full, the function of defilement would lack power.
Yet, since purity is full, there is the efficacy of manifesting what appears to be contrary to it.
It is known with certainty that even those heavily defiled possess the functional utility of being compliant with their inherent nature.
The answer is:
all Buddhas are permeated by the influence of great compassion and great vows.
Therefore, the nature of the Dharma-realm, which is contrary to the arising of defilement,
can cause those with the appropriate capacity to perceive this vision.
Sentient beings have no weariness toward the mundane and naturally delight in the habit of aspiring toward the sacred.
Therefore, the nature conforms to and conceals its boundless pure functions, so as not to allow the Buddhas to simultaneously reflect them; for there would be no pure vessel to reflect them.
Thus, the Great Sage relinquishes [this manifestation] to indicate that the capacity [of beings] possesses defiled qualities that can be perceived.
Those of lower capacity seek it and can be transformed through clarity.
Therefore, while the purity and fullness do not obstruct the presence of defiled qualities,
the weight of defilement prevents the manifestation of pure functions.
Regarding the three kinds of the nature of discrimination,
there are also two types:
first, the pure nature of discrimination.
Second is the defiled and turbid nature of discrimination.
As for what is called the pure nature of discrimination,
it refers to that very purity within the dharmas of the dependent nature.
All virtues that benefit others are,
from the perspective of that internal non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
termed "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*); that is to say, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) which cognizes the various distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
He fully knows, without exception, all the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings; furthermore,
he manifests the signs of the five supernatural powers and the three wheels of activity,
and assumes the forms of the six destinies and the four modes of birth according to his transformative response.
Ultimately, relying upon the wisdom of internal realization,
one gives rise to the knowledge that employs those teachings;
having realized this for oneself, one reveals it to those who have not yet heard it.
Such matters as these are all termed the dharmas of the pure *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that although boundless phenomena arise, [they are all of this nature].
Furthermore, because it is ultimately unstained by the world and accomplishes its tasks spontaneously without effort, it is called "pure.
This very pure awareness is termed "discrimination" because its functions vary according to different objects.

Furthermore, by confronting conditions to gather and transform others so that they attain purity, one distinguishes for them the virtue of such gathering and benefiting; therefore, it is called the "pure nature of discrimination.
As for what is called the "defiled nature of the dharma of discrimination":
Within that very defiled dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
there exist phenomena that appear as form, consciousness, objects, and so forth;
for what reason are they all termed "appearances" (*pratibhāsa*)?
Because they all arise through the power of a single mind based on habitual perfuming,
they are merely phenomena that resemble the mind;
since they are not real, they are termed "resemblances."
Thus, at the moment when this semblance of consciousness arises as a single thought-instant,
it arises simultaneously with the semblance of objects;
therefore, at the very moment of its arising, one does not realize that these semblances of objects and semblances of forms are empty signs produced by the mind and lack substantial reality.
Because they do not know this, they engage in false discrimination, grasping at the unreal as real.
Due to this false grasping, objects evolve from the mind and all become perceived as substantial realities;
this is precisely what is seen by ordinary people at present.
When grasping in this manner,
it immediately perfumes the mind moment by moment, thereby forming the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
upon that, one grasps again, thereby forming the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
In this way, moment by moment, false imaginings arise from one another.
Question: Once it has been established that the nature of discrimination and the dependent nature arise alternately from one another, [what follows?]
What is the distinction?
The answer is:
it is the phenomenon of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
The nature of the mind arises based on habitual perfuming;
it is merely a manifestation of the mind, its essence being empty and devoid of reality.
As for phenomena of the nature of discrimination:
Because of ignorance, one does not know that phenomena dependent on others are empty;
thus, one falsely clings to them as real entities.
Therefore, although there is no arising of distinct substantial natures, there remains a distinction between the empty and the real.
Therefore, it is said that these are the phenomena of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, there is another meaning by which the three natures are elucidated.
The equality of the essence of mind is termed "the nature of reality" (*tathatā*).
The essence of mind serves as the basis upon which defilement and purity depend;
according to these two factors of defilement and purity, it is termed "the nature of dependence on others" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The fruit of the manifested false appearance is called the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), discrimination itself is categorized as the three natures.
The first is the pure portion,
which refers to the true nature within defilement, termed "true reality" (*tathatā*).
The second is the impure portion.
That is to say, the seeds of the habitual tendencies of defiled dharmas and their results as empty appearances constitute the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The non-duality of these two natures in their union constitutes the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Question: When deluded discrimination arises resembling consciousness,
does the mental consciousness as a whole discriminate all six sense objects?
[Question: Do the six consciousnesses each individually discern a single object? [Answer:
When the five consciousnesses perceive an object, they arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
When visual consciousness perceives what appears as form,
it is simultaneously the deluded attachment of conceptualization by the single mental consciousness.
The other consciousnesses are also like this.
Therefore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is generally able to differentiate and falsely grasp the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*),
whereas the five consciousnesses can only apprehend the five sense-objects without giving rise to differentiation or false grasping.
Question: Regarding those who falsely cling to the five sense objects as being real,
does this refer to the five consciousnesses?
This refers to the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The answer is:
within the Mahāyāna, no distinction is made between the five sensory consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness.
Whatever can perform discrimination is entirely termed the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The above has concluded the explanation of the second [section], which clarifies the objects of observation for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Next, the third [section] shall clarify the essential characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Within this, there are further two sections clarifying the meaning:
first, elucidating the essential characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in their defiled state;
second, elucidating the essential characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by means of the three natures in their purified state.
First, within the three natures that are subject to defilement, a further threefold classification is established:
first, an exposition based on the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
second, a manifestation based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and third, a demonstration through contrast with the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the clarification of the essential characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā with respect to the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*):
one first enters śamatha from vipaśyanā.
As for what is called "vipaśyanā":
One should contemplate the five aggregates and the six external sense objects;
regarding each and every phenomenon, one should form this thought:
"This phenomenon which I now perceive as having a real form, substance, and solid obstruction, existing inherently in this way—"
However, because there is ignorance when the consciousness has its fruit,
one does not know that this dharma is empty.
Because one does not know that the dharma is empty, [one remains deluded].
One immediately gives rise to deluded thoughts and clings to them as real;
for this reason, at present, one’s mind is firmly convinced that they are actual facts.
Furthermore, one should reflect as follows:
Since beginningless time, due to the grasping at reality,
one gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion toward all objects;
thereby creating various karmas that bring about birth and death.
Being unable to emerge from it on their own—
those who form this understanding are said to have entered the gate of contemplation.
It is not that after having performed this contemplation, one further forms this thought:
"I now know that it is due to the false imaginings of ignorance—
taking what is unreal to be real— that I have been wandering through birth and death."
Now, why do you still wish to believe this deluded and false mind? Therefore,
you must oppose it and forcefully contemplate all phenomena as being merely manifestations of the mind— empty forms without reality.
It is just as a child who loves the reflection in a mirror and thinks it is a real person;
yet the nature of this reflected image is not real,
existing only because the child’s own mind considers it to be real.
That which is called "real" is in fact without reality.
I am now likewise so;
because of delusion, I take what is unreal to be real.
If one firmly grasps within the mind that something is real,
